fixes.explanation: Luke says, "And Peter followed at a distance." He's not gone, but he's not up close either. I think he's trying to stay near without standing out.
That would be a bold walk, friend, but it's not what Luke tells us. He says Peter followed "…at a distance." Right at His side is close, and a distance is not close.
Luke says they seized Jesus and led Him away. He says nothing about Peter being tied up. Peter follows at a distance, and later he sits down among those at the fire.
She looks at him intently as he sits in the firelight. Then she says, "This man also was with Him…" She means Jesus, the One who was just seized.
Luke doesn't say anything like that. She says, "This man also was with Him…" and the "Him" is Jesus. Nothing in her words is about a job in the high priest's house.
That's not what she says, baker. She says, "This man also was with Him…" Her words are about being with Jesus, not about being a stranger.

Right, baker. The servant girl says Peter was with Jesus, and Peter answers, "Woman, I do not know Him…" She asks about being with Jesus, and he says he doesn't even know Him. That's the first of three times in this courtyard that Peter denies it.

Luke says, "And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed." The rooster crows right while Peter is still talking. That timing is something, friend. That rooster showed up like it had a meeting on the calendar.
No guard grabs anybody in these verses. Peter is talking, and "…immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed." The rooster is what Luke gives us, not a hand.
Luke says, "And the Lord turned and looked at Peter." Jesus is the Lord here. The text gives us the look, and then Luke says Peter remembers the word the Lord had spoken to him.

The Lord told Peter, "Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times." Count them in the courtyard: the servant girl, then someone else, then another man. That's three, just like the Lord said.
Luke doesn't say Peter complains. He says Peter "…went outside and wept bitterly." I think that's grief, not grumbling, friend.
Luke says, "At daybreak the council of the elders of the people, both the chief priests and scribes, met together." The night is over, and the council gathers. Daybreak is when they meet together.
Luke says the council of the elders of the people is made up of "…both the chief priests and scribes…" They meet together at daybreak. Then they lead Jesus into their Sanhedrin.

Not here, friend. Pilate, governor of Judea, and Herod, ruler of Galilee (Luke 3:1), aren't named in this meeting. Luke says this council is "…both the chief priests and scribes…" Those are the ones he lists.
It's the opposite, friend. When they say, "If You are the Christ, tell us," Jesus answers, "If I tell you, you will not believe." I think that means telling them isn't going to change anything.
Right. The council says, "If You are the Christ, tell us." Jesus answers, "If I tell you, you will not believe." Believing is the very thing He says isn't coming.
Luke doesn't say that. Jesus says, "And if I ask you a question, you will not answer." Nothing in His words is about laughing.
After Jesus speaks of the Son of Man, the whole council asks, "Are You then the Son of God?" Luke says they all asked Him that. Jesus replies, "You say that I am."
